headline: High risk of shared-workspace data leakage and cascading errors; prompt injection is moderate, compliance risk is medium.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and uses shared memory by default; Dify can ingest uploaded knowledge base files and conversation context. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other’s outputs as trusted text. The pairwise pathway is not fully documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF CrewAI writes attacker-controlled text into the shared working directory and Dify reads it as prompt material
IF Dify ingests CrewAI output into a workflow step without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files into prompts
Add a provenance tag to all inter-agent artifacts
Review any file-to-prompt connectors before enabling them

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and has broad filesystem/network access; Dify touches knowledge base content and conversation logs. If they share a workspace or datastore, sensitive inputs can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs or logs. The profiles do not prove a shared OS workspace, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same host directory or datastore
IF either agent logs or re-uploads the other agent’s files or prompts
mitigations: Use separate workspaces and credentials
Turn off verbose logging for shared artifacts
Restrict file permissions on any exchanged files
Redact secrets before passing outputs between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read and write the filesystem, and use broad network egress. CrewAI’s shared state is developer-defined, while Dify shares state via server datastore; if they target the same mutable resources, concurrent writes can collide and corrupt files or workflow state. Because both have unrestricted write surfaces, the conflict is dangerous by default once co-located.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or datastore
IF either agent mutates shared files without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable one agent’s write path during handoff
Use immutable artifacts between steps
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework with shared memory, and Dify’s agent/workflow model can consume tool and model outputs directly. That makes it plausible for Dify to treat CrewAI-produced text as authoritative without verification, causing errors to cascade into downstream actions or responses. The interaction is not documented, so I choose the higher severity.
conditions: IF Dify uses CrewAI output as a workflow input without validation
IF downstream tools act on unverified CrewAI-generated facts
mitigations: Insert a human review step before actions
Require schema validation on inter-agent outputs
Add source citations to every handoff
Reject outputs that lack confidence markers
requires-engineering: implement verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, while Dify stores knowledge base content and conversation logs. If regulated or sensitive data is routed through both, differing retention and logging behaviors can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not show a specific residency or certification conflict, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Dify conversation logs or knowledge base files
IF CrewAI passes secrets or personal data into Dify-managed storage
mitigations: Classify data before routing it
Avoid placing regulated data in logs
Set retention limits on both systems
Delete test conversations after validation
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies
